title: Companies Are Becoming a Series of Loops: AI Can Climb the Hill, but Humans Must Choose the Next Mountain
dek: Companies are being reshaped into interlocking loops; loops can push current operations to a local optimum, but after a plateau, choosing the next mountain still requires human intuition.
why: A structural take from an a16z partner: companies will be rewritten by loops, and the biggest consumer AI opportunity lies in joy, not efficiency. The views are often counterintuitive, useful for stress-testing your own product roadmap.
who: Founders and product leaders who are using AI to reshape their products or reorganize company processes, as well as investors interested in AI's impact on employment and consumer opportunities.
skip: If short on time, you can skip the final book list, life mottos, and DJ anecdotes without missing the AI analysis.

points.h: AI Era Won't Replicate Winner-Take-All Dynamics
points.body: The AI era won't follow the mobile internet's winner-take-all pattern: network effects once pushed search and social toward one or two players, but each layer of the AI stack now has about 20 relevant participants. Two years ago, everyone thought programming agents would eventually leave a single winner, yet Claude Code, Codex, Lovable, and Replit are all advancing simultaneously. Anish says the most cutting-edge people in the labs believe what's actually happening is autocatalytic effects—using new technology to improve your own processes—rather than recursive self-improvement, so there won't be a runaway winner that swallows everyone. The lesson for founders: don't bet solely on a full-stack giant; each layer (models, agents, interfaces) still has a long-term position.

points.h: CEOs Want Bigger Companies, Not Fewer Employees
points.body: Employees probably don't need to over-worry about being replaced by AI, not because the technology isn't strong enough, but because CEOs are incentivized by growth, not shrinkage. Sundar doesn't want to run a more efficient $4 trillion company; he wants to build a $40 trillion one. A Google executive friend told Anish that the company hasn't laid off staff; instead, it's using AI to compress a two-year roadmap into three months, and the current challenge is 'what to add to the roadmap.' When execution becomes less scarce, attention shifts from saving labor to finding new things to do for larger goals.

points.h: Companies Become Loops; the Next Step Needs Humans
points.body: The company form is shifting from a list of roles and departments to a cascade of loops: starting with automation of individual workflows, then functional loops, then crossing business units, and eventually loops running most of the company's operations. Loops continuously produce outputs that become inputs for the next layer, and some mechanism feeds signals back to the CEO—when to adjust business entities, when to change strategy. This mechanism helps the company climb to a local maximum, but after a plateau, human intuition is needed for out-of-distribution thinking to place the organization at the foot of the next mountain. Letting AI directly come up with an idea that can make a million dollars often fails because humans can set the direction; AI only sweeps along the established slope.

points.h: Users Want to Spend Time, Not Save It
points.body: Silicon Valley's default assumption is that AI's value is efficiency, but Anish sees this as a misjudgment: most people don't really want to save time; they want to spend it on things that bring connection, love, progress, and fun. Historically, the biggest products have been entertainment and social, so the consumer AI opportunity isn't 'saving a few more minutes' but creating loops that make people feel more connected, more loved, or that they're making progress or having fun. He criticizes that technology over the past 40 years has extended intellect but hardly touched the soul; fitting AI into these desires is a product design challenge, not a model capability challenge.

points.h: AI Is Decoupling Skills from Desires
points.body: Anish believes AI is more than a productivity tool; it's like an emotional and spiritual interface—it can separate 'skills' from 'desires.' People who want to make music are no longer blocked by 'not knowing how to play piano'; those who want to write programs don't need to first learn to a professional level; personal identity is thus amplified. He recalls that high-risk environments in the 1950s-60s greatly stimulated human potential, and believes the current world is in a low-risk state, where AI has the chance to lift GDP growth from 2% to 10-15%—provided it raises not just the speed of individual steps but the scale of what groups dare to imagine.

points.h: Ideas Too Small Now Fail to Raise Funding
points.body: Investment criteria have reversed within three years. In the past, if a project was too ambitious, funds would often say a $100 million seed round was too much; today at a16z, the reverse standard applies—if an idea, even with AI help, can only be that small, they simply don't invest. 'Unbounded ambition' has become the core value for screening companies. Marc Andreessen's phrasing: we either go to the moon or leave a moon-sized crater.

points.h: Weekly Small Releases Build Product Intuition
points.body: The most direct advice for product people is the old saying: build more. Pick a project you tell no one about, the smaller the better, treat it as a 'chassis,' run each new model through it, ship the result, and discuss it with people—this is the path to building AI intuition. The pace just needs to be one small release per week; intensity is unsustainable. Anish himself used Codex to make a Mother's Day slideshow for his wife: pulling material from texts and photo albums, auto-scoring music, and finally generating a 20-page retrospective of their relationship, even digging up old texts from their first date. The thing is small, but such works let you repeatedly taste AI's 'joy moments'—once you taste them, your mindset never goes back.
